prompt.context: Our client is a large European airplane manufacturer that is developing a new jumbo jet, which will be able to hold approximately 800-900 people. Parts for the plane are manufactured in multiple sites across Europe. The client has provided the following information on site production: Cockpits are produced in Northern Spain; the fuselage is produced in Northern Germany; wings are produced in Northern England; landing gears/interior are produced in Southern France.
prompt.question: The client has asked us to determine where it is most economical to assemble the plane.

clarifying_info.q: What are the major cost components of assembly?
clarifying_info.a: Labor accounts for about 70% of total assembly costs; transportation accounts for the other 30%. Disregard other costs such as real estate.

clarifying_info.q: How do labor costs compare between France and the Czech Republic?
clarifying_info.a: Labor in France is 1.5 times higher than labor in the Czech Republic.

clarifying_info.q: How significant is the per-mile cost of transporting parts?
clarifying_info.a: The marginal cost of each extra mile transported is close to zero. The most significant transportation cost is the labor associated with loading parts.

clarifying_info.q: Which parts are easiest or hardest to load for transport?
clarifying_info.a: The interior and landing gears are the easiest to pack of all four parts; the fuselage is the hardest (most expensive) to pack.

clarifying_info.q: What is the annual demand and how long does it take to assemble one plane?
clarifying_info.a: Demand is 200 planes per year; it takes 9 months to assemble one plane; one plane requires a space of about 300 ft x 300 ft.

framework: Identify candidate assembly locations (existing manufacturing sites vs. low-cost alternatives such as Eastern Europe)
Break total assembly cost into major drivers: labor (70%) and transportation (30%)
Compare labor costs across candidate locations
Compare transportation costs across candidate locations, noting that loading/unloading cost dominates per-mile cost
Assess capabilities: labor skill availability, infrastructure
Determine optimal location based on cost comparison
Size the required facility given production rate and assembly cycle time

questions.prompt: Which locations should be considered for assembly, and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should suggest both existing manufacturing sites (France is central to the four sites) and low-cost alternatives such as Eastern European countries (e.g., Czech Republic) with cheaper labor. France is attractive because landing gears/interior are already there, reducing one transport leg; Czech Republic is attractive for significantly lower labor costs.

questions.prompt: Given that labor is 70% of cost and France labor is 1.5x Czech Republic labor, which location has lower total costs?
questions.guidance: Labor savings in Czech Republic are decisive. France labor = 1.5x Czech. Czech saves 33% on labor relative to France (1 - 1/1.5). Since labor is 70% of total cost, Czech saves ~0.70 x 33% = ~23% of total cost. Transportation costs do not favor France because the dominant transport cost is loading/unloading, not distance; and the parts already at France (interior/gears) are the cheapest to load anyway, so France's advantage on transport is minimal. Net recommendation: Czech Republic.

math.setup: Labor cost ratio: France = 1.5 x Czech. Czech Republic labor cost saving vs France = (1 - 1/1.5) = 33%. Labor share of total cost = 70%. Transportation share = 30%.
steps: Labor saving as % of total cost = 70% x 33% = ~23%
Transport costs: marginal per-mile cost ~0; dominant cost is loading. Parts already in France (interior/gears) are cheapest to load, so France transport advantage is minimal
Net: Czech Republic total cost is materially lower
math.answer: Czech Republic is more economical; labor savings of ~23% of total cost outweigh any transport advantage France might have.

questions.prompt: How large should the assembly facility be? (Demand: 200 planes/year; assembly time: 9 months; footprint: 300 ft x 300 ft per plane)
questions.guidance: Calculate the number of planes in assembly at any one time, then multiply by per-plane footprint.

math.setup: Annual demand = 200 planes. Assembly cycle = 9 months = 0.75 years. Footprint per plane = 300 ft x 300 ft = 90,000 sq ft.
steps: Planes in facility at any time = 200 planes/year x 0.75 years = 150 planes
Total facility area = 150 planes x 90,000 sq ft/plane = 13,500,000 sq ft
math.answer: The facility must be approximately 13.5 million sq ft (13.5M sq ft).

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors beyond labor and transportation costs should the client consider when choosing an assembly location?

categories.name: Infrastructure
ideas: Airport or airfield access for test flights
Road/rail capacity for oversized part transport
Proximity to suppliers for non-manufactured components

categories.name: Tax & Regulatory
ideas: Corporate tax rates and incentives by country
EU regional development grants or subsidies
Customs and import duties for intra-EU parts movement

categories.name: Strategic
ideas: Long-term cost trajectory (wage inflation in Czech Republic vs France)

recommendation: Assemble the plane in the Czech Republic, where labor costs are approximately 33% lower than in France; since labor represents 70% of total assembly cost, this yields roughly a 23% reduction in total assembly cost

Transportation costs do not favor France meaningfully, because the dominant transportation expense is loading/unloading labor rather than distance, and the parts already located in France (landing gears/interior) are the least expensive to load
The facility should be approximately 13.5 million sq ft to accommodate 150 planes in simultaneous assembly (200 planes/year x 0.75-year cycle)
risks: Labor skill in Czech Republic may not match Western European aerospace standards — a workforce training investment may be required
Wage inflation in Eastern Europe could erode the cost advantage over time
Transporting large structural components (especially fuselage) to Czech Republic adds logistical complexity
next_steps: Assess Czech Republic labor pool quality and training requirements for aerospace assembly
Model 10-year total cost of ownership including wage inflation scenarios

Evaluate Germany as an alternative: fuselage is the costliest part to transport and is produced in Germany, so proximity savings on fuselage loading may partially offset higher German labor vs Czech Republic
Explore EU subsidies and tax incentives available for establishing a manufacturing facility in Czech Republic
